New Jersey Will Require Online Casinos to Monitor and Intervene With At-Risk Players

Published October 22, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport announced new rules requiring online casino and sportsbook operators licensed by the state's Division of Gaming Enforcement to actively monitor customer accounts for signs of problem gambling and intervene directly when specific behavioral thresholds are tripped. The state is describing it as the first mandatory, data-driven monitoring and intervention framework of its kind among U.S. gambling regulators.

What the rule actually requires

Operators must review an account when a customer hits any of a defined set of triggers, including depositing more than $10,000 within 24 hours or $100,000 over 90 days, recording at least $1 million in betting turnover within 90 days, visiting the state's self-exclusion page three times in 30 days without registering, canceling a withdrawal request three times within 10 days, requesting a second cooling-off period within 45 days, or showing a 50% jump in login time compared to the prior two weeks. Any customer flagged this way is placed on a monitoring list and routed through a three-stage intervention process: an initial email outlining responsible-gambling tools such as deposit and loss limits, a required educational video before the customer can resume play if concerning patterns continue, and finally direct phone or video contact along with a referral to a responsible-gambling professional. Accounts can be suspended after repeated failed contact attempts or closed outright if a gambling problem is confirmed.

DGE Interim Director Mary Jo Flaherty said the framework is designed to "ensure early intervention and support, tiered to individual need." Gov. Mikie Sherrill framed the move as part of New Jersey's broader approach to online gambling oversight, saying the state "continues to lead the way in developing data-driven best practices for internet gaming and online sports wagering."

Why now

The announcement follows reporting earlier this year that a FanDuel VIP customer with a documented problematic betting pattern received a personalized promotional video from an MLB player, prompting a lawsuit alleging the operator encouraged his gambling activity rather than curbing it. New Jersey regulators have also been active on enforcement more broadly; DGE records cited alongside this announcement show a $78,000 fine against Penn Entertainment's theScore Bet operation this same week for accepting unauthorized wagers. Luis Del Orbe, executive director of the Council on Compulsive Gambling of New Jersey, welcomed tighter intervention requirements but cautioned that overly aggressive restrictions could push some customers toward unregulated offshore platforms that offer none of the same safeguards.

Why it matters to players

New Jersey's online casino and sports betting market is one of the largest and most mature in the country, and rules written there often become a reference point for other states' regulators. Players with accounts at New Jersey-licensed operators should expect more proactive outreach — emails, required videos, or direct contact — if their deposit size, turnover, or account behavior crosses the thresholds above, rather than relying solely on self-service tools like deposit limits or self-exclusion that a player has to activate themselves.
